context.heading: Betrothed, but not yet together
context.body: Mary was betrothed (mnēsteuō, "pledged in marriage") to Joseph. Jewish betrothal was far more binding than a modern engagement: the couple were legally husband and wife, though they did not yet live together. That is why ending it required a divorce (v. 19), and why Joseph is already called her husband.

context.heading: A pattern broken on purpose
context.body: For fifteen verses the genealogy repeats one active verb, gennaō: "Abraham was the father of Isaac", and so on. At Jesus the pattern breaks. Joseph is "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus", with a passive verb and a feminine "whom" in Greek that points to Mary alone. Matthew prepares readers for the virgin birth before he tells it.

context.heading: A name that carries a mission
context.body: Jesus is the Greek form of Yeshua (Joshua), meaning "the LORD saves". The angel spells it out: He will save (sōzō) His people from their sins. Many hoped for rescue from Rome, but the angel names a deeper enemy. The first Joshua led Israel into the land; this one deals with what kept them from God.

theology.title: Promises kept across centuries
theology.body: The genealogy falls into three sets of fourteen: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to Christ. It reads like a slow sermon. God promised Abraham blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:3) and David an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and through failure, exile and silence He kept both.

theology.title: Grace runs through a crooked line
theology.body: The family tree includes a deceiver, an adulterous king, idolatrous rulers and Gentile women. Matthew does not airbrush it. God's saving plan never depended on a clean pedigree, which is good news for every reader whose own family story is complicated.

theology.title: Truly human, conceived by the Spirit
theology.body: Jesus has a real legal lineage through Joseph and a real human birth through Mary, yet He is conceived by the Holy Spirit (v. 20). Isaiah 7:14 is fulfilled not only in a sign but in a Person: God Himself has come near. The Apostles' Creed echoes this chapter almost word for word.

application.title: Right without being cruel
application.body: Joseph believed Mary had been unfaithful, and the law gave him grounds to shame her. He chose a quiet divorce instead, then changed course entirely when God spoke. Being right did not require him to humiliate anyone.
application.question: Where do you have a legitimate grievance that you are tempted to make as public as possible?

application.title: Your family story is not final
application.body: Matthew names Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and "the wife of Uriah" without hiding why they are memorable. God wove even scandal into the Messiah's line. The worst chapter in your family's past does not decide what God can do with its future.
application.question: What part of your family history have you assumed disqualifies you from being used by God?

context.heading: A shepherd, not a tyrant
context.body: The chief priests quote Micah 5:2 and blend in 2 Samuel 5:2: a ruler who will shepherd (poimainō) Israel. The verb means to tend, feed and protect a flock. It stands in sharp contrast with Herod, who would soon slaughter Bethlehem's boys to protect his own throne.

context.heading: Experts who stayed home
context.body: The chief priests and scribes knew at once where the Messiah would be born. Bethlehem was only about six miles (10 km) from Jerusalem, yet Matthew records no one going with the Magi. Knowing the right verse and seeking the King turned out to be two different things.

context.heading: Why "a Nazarene"?
context.body: No Old Testament verse says the Messiah "will be called a Nazarene", and Matthew says "the prophets", plural. Many scholars think he is summarizing a theme: Nazareth was an obscure, looked-down-on village (John 1:46), fitting prophecies of a despised servant (Isaiah 53:3). Some also hear a play on netser, the "branch" from Jesse's root (Isaiah 11:1).

theology.title: God draws the nations to His Son
theology.body: The first worshipers in Matthew are Gentile outsiders led by a star. Isaiah 60:3 promised that nations would come to Israel's light, and Psalm 72:10–11 pictures kings bringing gifts. The Gospel that ends with "make disciples of all nations" (28:19) begins with the nations already arriving.

theology.title: Sovereign over a tyrant's rage
theology.body: Herod has soldiers, informants and power, yet he cannot touch the child. God guides by star, by Scripture and by dreams, and outmaneuvers every move. "Out of Egypt I called My Son" (Hosea 11:1) shows Jesus reliving Israel's story, this time faithfully.

theology.title: God hears Rachel weeping
theology.body: Matthew does not gloss over the massacre. He quotes Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping for her children, a verse that sits just before Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant. God does not stop every evil in a fallen world, but He records the grief and is already moving toward the rescue He promised.

application.title: Worship with a price tag
application.body: The Magi traveled for months and opened treasure for a toddler in an ordinary house. Their worship cost them time, money and comfort. Worship that never inconveniences us sounds suspiciously like Herod's polite "so that I too may go and worship Him" (verse 8).
application.question: What would worship cost you this week if it cost you anything at all?

application.title: Insiders can miss it
application.body: The scribes had the right answer in seconds and never walked six miles to see if it was true. Familiarity with the Bible can quietly replace responding to it.
application.question: What truth do you know so well that you've stopped acting on it?

context.heading: A rethinking that turns a life
context.body: Metanoeō joins "after" and "mind": a rethinking that redirects the whole life. It carries the Old Testament idea of shuv, turning back to God. John's baptism was public, so it meant admitting before your neighbors that being born into Israel was not enough.

context.heading: Snakes fleeing a fire
context.body: John calls the Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers (echidna). Picture snakes slithering away from a brush fire in the Judean wilderness: they are running from coming wrath, not changing. It also mocks their pride in ancestry; their family resemblance, he implies, is closer to the serpent's than to Abraham's.

context.heading: Stones and sons
context.body: Many scholars note a likely wordplay in Hebrew and Aramaic, where "stones" (abanim) and "sons" (banim) sound alike. God can raise up children (teknon) for Abraham from rocks lying by the river. Descent from Abraham guaranteed nothing; God is free to create a people, as He once formed Adam from dust.

theology.title: The One who pours out the Spirit
theology.body: John says One mightier is coming who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (v. 11). The prophets promised a day when God would pour out His Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28). John's water was preparation; Jesus brings the reality. Christians read the "fire" as purifying, as judgment, or as both.

theology.title: Standing where sinners stand
theology.body: Jesus insists on baptism "to fulfill all righteousness" (v. 15). The One who needed no repentance steps into the water as Israel's representative, siding with sinners from His first public act. It foreshadows the cross, where the sinless One would take the place of the guilty (2 Corinthians 5:21).

application.title: Fruit, not pedigree
application.body: John was unimpressed by religious background. The issue was not who your parents were or which church you grew up in, but whether your life bears fruit that fits repentance (verse 8). Heritage is a gift, not a credential.
application.question: If someone shadowed you for an ordinary Tuesday, what evidence of a changed mind would they find?

application.title: Loved before the résumé
application.body: The Father says "This is My beloved Son" before Jesus has preached a sermon or healed anyone. His identity came first, and His work flowed from it. Many of us reverse that order and wear ourselves out trying to earn what can only be received.
application.question: How would your work change if you started each day already accepted rather than trying to earn it?

context.heading: Scripture quoted, then twisted
context.body: The devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12 accurately but bends its purpose, turning a promise of protection into a dare to force God's hand. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16, recalling Israel testing God at Massah (Exodus 17:7). Knowing verses is not the same as reading them the way God meant them.

context.heading: Galilee of the Gentiles
context.body: Matthew quotes Isaiah 9:1–2 about Zebulun and Naphtali, the first northern territories swallowed by Assyria in the 700s BC. Galilee had become a land mixed with the ethnē, the Gentile nations, and Judeans looked down on it. Isaiah promised that the region that first fell into darkness would be first to see the great light.

context.heading: A kingdom that has come near
context.body: Engizō means to approach or draw near; the perfect tense here (ēngiken) says the kingdom has arrived close and stays close. Jesus uses the same summary as John (3:2), but on His lips it means more. The King Himself is standing in front of them.

theology.title: The obedient Son where others fell
theology.body: Adam fell in a garden of plenty; Israel grumbled in the wilderness. Jesus, starving after forty days, refuses every shortcut. Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. His obedience is more than an example; it is credited to all who trust Him (Romans 5:19).

theology.title: Light that starts at the margins
theology.body: Jesus does not launch His ministry in the temple courts of Jerusalem but in despised Galilee, among fishermen and the sick. His fame spreads to Syria and the Decapolis (vv. 24–25). God's kingdom moves outward from the edges, the way Isaiah said it would.

application.title: Temptation aims at real needs
application.body: Hunger was real, and bread is not evil. The temptation was to meet a legitimate need on His own terms, outside the Father's timing. Most temptations still work this way: rest, approval and security pursued by a shortcut.
application.question: Which good desire in your life are you most tempted to satisfy by a shortcut?

application.title: Nets still wet
application.body: Peter and Andrew left their nets; James and John left a boat and their father (verses 20, 22). Following Jesus is not added on top of our plans; it reorders them. For most people that will not mean quitting a job, but changing whom the job ultimately serves.
application.question: What would be hardest for you to set down if Jesus asked for it today?

context.heading: Salt that turns foolish
context.body: The verb behind "loses its savor" is mōrainō, literally "to become foolish" (our word moron shares the root). Salt gathered near the Dead Sea was often mixed with other minerals; once moisture leached out the real salt, what remained looked like salt but did nothing. Disciples who lose their distinctiveness become, in Jesus' word, foolish.

context.heading: Fulfill, not abolish
context.body: Plēroō means to fill full, to bring to completion. Jesus neither discards the law nor merely keeps it; He is the goal it was pointing toward. Christians discuss how each part of Moses' law applies today, but agree that Jesus is its final interpreter and fulfillment.

context.heading: The second mile
context.body: Angareuō was a technical term for requisition: a Roman soldier could legally force a civilian to carry his gear for one mile. Simon of Cyrene is "forced" with the same verb to carry Jesus' cross (27:32). Jesus tells His hearers to volunteer a second mile, turning resentful compliance into free generosity toward an occupier.

theology.title: The Lawgiver speaks for Himself
theology.body: Prophets said, "Thus says the LORD." Jesus says, "But I tell you" again and again (vv. 22–44), placing His word on the level of the law given at Sinai. Only God can authoritatively explain God's law, and Jesus does so without hesitation.

theology.title: Sun on the evil and good
theology.body: Jesus grounds love for enemies in God's own character: He makes His sun rise on the evil and the good (v. 45). God's daily kindness is not a reward for good behavior. Loving enemies is a call to resemble the Father, which is why the chapter ends, "as your heavenly Father is perfect."

application.title: Contempt has a vocabulary
application.body: Jesus traces murder back to contempt: calling someone "Raca" (empty-headed) or a fool (verse 22). The insults we type in a group chat or mutter in traffic are not small. They reveal what we think a person is worth.
application.question: Who have you quietly written off as worthless, even if you would never say it out loud?

application.title: Make it right before you worship
application.body: Jesus says to leave your gift at the altar and go be reconciled first (verses 23–24). Worship does not paper over a broken relationship you are able to repair. Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do this week is a hard phone call.
application.question: Who might have something against you that you are hoping time will quietly fix?

context.heading: Stamped "paid in full"
context.body: Apechō was a business term written on receipts in Greek papyri, meaning "paid in full". Those who give, pray or fast to be seen have already been paid (apechō) their reward. The applause is the entire payment; nothing more is coming.

context.heading: Bread for the day
context.body: Epiousios, translated "daily", is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer, so its meaning is debated: "necessary for existence", "for today" or "for the coming day". Each fits a day laborer's world, where many were paid each evening and bought tomorrow's food with it.

context.heading: A generous eye
context.body: Haplous means single or undivided. In Jewish idiom a "good eye" meant generosity and an "evil eye" meant stinginess or envy (see 20:15). Set between treasure (vv. 19–21) and money (v. 24), Jesus' saying is likely about what our gaze fixes on and whether we hold possessions with an open hand.

theology.title: A Father who sees in secret
theology.body: Jesus calls God "Father" about a dozen times in this chapter. He is not a distant auditor tallying public performance but a Father who sees what no one else sees and delights to reward it (vv. 4, 6, 18). Prayer begins with relationship: "Our Father in heaven."

theology.title: His name and kingdom first
theology.body: The prayer's first three requests concern God, echoing the hope that His name would be honored among the nations (Ezekiel 36:23). Only then do we ask for bread, forgiveness and protection. God is not reluctant to meet our needs; He re-centers our priorities as we ask.

theology.title: The God who feeds sparrows
theology.body: Birds do not store food and wildflowers do not spin cloth, yet God feeds and clothes them (vv. 26–30), as Psalms 104 and 147 celebrate. If He tends grass that is burned tomorrow, He will not forget His children. Anxiety often grows from forgetting what He is like.

application.title: Check your audience
application.body: Few of us pray on street corners, but we may give, serve or post about our faith with one eye on who is watching. Jesus' test is simple: would you still do it if no one ever found out?
application.question: Which good habit of yours would quietly fade if it stopped being seen?

application.title: Money wants to be master
application.body: Jesus does not say you should not serve God and money; He says you cannot (verse 24). Money is pictured as a rival lord demanding loyalty. Where your money and attention go without thinking shows which one is winning.
application.question: If you scrolled through last month's spending, whose kingdom would it show you seeking first?

context.heading: A splinter and a beam
context.body: Jesus contrasts a karphos, a speck of straw or wood, with a dokos, a roof beam. The picture is deliberately absurd, the kind of humor a carpenter's son might use. The point is not that we may never correct anyone (v. 5) but that the work starts with ourselves.

context.heading: Dogs and pigs
context.body: Dogs in that world were mostly scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean animals. Jesus warns against pressing holy things on people who are openly treating them with contempt. Placed right after "do not judge", it keeps the balance: discernment is still required.

context.heading: Busy, but lawless
context.body: People who prophesied and did miracles in Jesus' name are dismissed as workers of anomia, "lawlessness". It is a startling word for people so full of religious activity. Their problem was not a lack of spiritual power but that they never did the Father's will (v. 21), and Jesus never knew them.

theology.title: How much more the Father
theology.body: If flawed parents do not hand a child a stone when asked for bread, how much more will the Father give good things (v. 11)? Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater, a familiar rabbinic method. Prayer rests on God's goodness, not on finding the right formula.

theology.title: Jesus at the center of judgment
theology.body: "On that day" (v. 22) is the prophets' language for the day of the LORD. Jesus places Himself at its center: people plead with Him, and His verdict decides. Matthew's readers would recognize Him taking a role that belongs to God alone.

application.title: Start with your own eye
application.body: Jesus does not forbid helping with someone's speck; He forbids doing it with a beam in your own eye. People who have honestly faced their own sin usually correct others more gently and more accurately.
application.question: What criticism you often make of others might actually describe you?

application.title: Hearing is not building
application.body: Both builders heard the same sermon. The difference showed only when the storm hit, and it came down to doing what they heard. Sermons, podcasts and devotionals become foundation only when they reach behavior.
application.question: What did you last hear from Scripture that you have not yet actually done?

context.heading: "I am not worthy"
context.body: The centurion says he is not hikanos, "fit" or "sufficient", for Jesus to come under his roof. Devout Jews avoided entering Gentile homes, and he may be sparing Jesus that problem. As an officer over roughly a hundred men, he understands authority: a word from Jesus is enough (v. 9).

context.heading: He carried our weaknesses
context.body: Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4: He took our infirmities (astheneia) and carried our diseases. That is the Suffering Servant passage, which also says He was pierced for our transgressions. Matthew sees the healings as previews of what Jesus' suffering would finally win: the undoing of sin and all its effects.

context.heading: Before the appointed time
context.body: The demons ask whether Jesus has come to torment them before the kairos, the appointed time. Kairos means a set or fitting moment, not just clock time. The demons know a day of judgment is fixed; what alarms them is that the Judge has arrived early.

theology.title: The Creator in the boat
theology.body: "Even the winds and the sea obey Him!" (v. 27). In the Psalms it is the LORD who stills the roaring seas (Psalm 65:7; 89:9; 107:29). The disciples ask, "What kind of man is this?" The Old Testament offers only one answer.

theology.title: A banquet from east and west
theology.body: Jesus says many Gentiles will feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (v. 11), echoing the great banquet of Isaiah 25:6. God's family is defined by faith, not birth. His warning to the "sons of the kingdom" is sobering for anyone leaning on religious heritage.

application.title: Read the cost first
application.body: A scribe offers to follow Jesus anywhere, and Jesus answers that He has nowhere to lay His head (verse 20). He is not turning the man away but showing him the bill before the meal. Enthusiasm that has not counted the cost tends to evaporate.
application.question: What comfort have you quietly made a condition of following Jesus?

application.title: What fear assumes
application.body: The disciples panicked with Jesus asleep in the same boat, and the storm was real. But fear pushed them toward a conclusion: He does not care (Mark 4:38 says it outright). Our anxieties often carry that same quiet accusation.
application.question: What does your current worry assume about whether Jesus cares?

context.heading: "Go and learn"
context.body: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, where eleos ("mercy") translates the Hebrew hesed, God's steadfast covenant love. Hosea rebuked people who kept the sacrifices while neglecting faithfulness. "Go and learn" was a phrase rabbis used to send a student back to study, a pointed thing to say to Pharisees.

context.heading: Guests of the bridegroom
context.body: Wedding feasts could last a week, and guests were excused from duties like fasting. By calling Himself the bridegroom (nymphios), Jesus takes up a picture the prophets used for God and Israel (Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). He also hints that the bridegroom will be taken away, and then His friends will fast.

context.heading: Reaching for the tassel
context.body: The woman touches the kraspedon of His cloak, probably one of the tassels Jews wore on garment corners to remember God's commands (Numbers 15:38–40). Her bleeding had likely left her ritually unclean for twelve years, cut off from worship and from touch. Jesus does not recoil; He calls her "daughter".

theology.title: Authority only God has
theology.body: Jesus tells a paralyzed man his sins are forgiven, and the scribes cry blasphemy, rightly assuming only God can forgive sins (Isaiah 43:25). Jesus then heals the visible problem to prove His authority over the invisible one. Matthew presents the forgiveness as the greater miracle.

theology.title: The God who goes looking
theology.body: Jesus came to call sinners, not the righteous (v. 13). That fits God's pattern from the beginning: He seeks people who hide (Genesis 3:9) and promises to search for the lost (Ezekiel 34:16). Grace is not a prize for the respectable but a rescue for the sick.

application.title: Notice who is at your table
application.body: Jesus ate at Matthew's house with people the respectable avoided, and took heat for it. In that culture a shared meal signaled acceptance. Our tables, group chats and friendships still show whom we think is worth our company.
application.question: Who would be surprised to get an invitation from you, and why haven't they?

application.title: The pray-er becomes the sent
application.body: Jesus sees the crowds as a harvest and tells His disciples to pray for workers (verses 37–38). In the next chapter, those same disciples are sent. Asking God to meet a need can be the first step in Him sending you to meet it.
application.question: What need do you keep praying about that you might be part of the answer to?

context.heading: Two sparrows for a penny
context.body: An assarion was a small copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius, the usual day's wage. Two sparrows sold for one, among the cheapest food in the market. Jesus says not one of them falls to the ground apart from the Father.

context.heading: A sword that divides homes
context.body: A machaira was a short sword or large knife. Jesus is not calling for violence; the next verses quote Micah 7:6, where family members turn against each other. The sword is the division His claims create when some in a household follow Him and others refuse.

context.heading: The road of the condemned
context.body: Before Jesus' own death, stauros ("cross") would bring Roman crucifixion to mind, where the condemned often carried the crossbeam to execution past jeering crowds. Rome had crucified many Jewish rebels. To take up your cross meant walking that road, surrendering any claim on your own life.

theology.title: Authority shared with the sent
theology.body: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and every sickness (v. 1), the very works He has just done in chapters 8–9. Whoever receives them receives Him, and whoever receives Him receives the Father (v. 40). God's mission now runs through ordinary messengers.

theology.title: Fear and comfort from one God
theology.body: Jesus says not to fear those who can kill the body but the One who can destroy soul and body in hell (v. 28). In the next breath He says this same God numbers their hairs. Holy fear and deep comfort come from the same Father.

application.title: Freely received, freely given
application.body: The disciples were not to charge for healing or turn their mission into a business (verse 8). Whatever God has given you, whether time, skill or forgiveness, is meant to keep moving outward.
application.question: What have you received from God that you have been treating as yours to keep?

application.title: Where you go quiet
application.body: Jesus speaks of acknowledging Him before others (verse 32). For most of us that test comes at a work lunch, a family dinner or a comment thread, not a courtroom. Silence is sometimes wisdom, and sometimes it is simply fear.
application.question: In which setting do you most often go quiet about Jesus, and why that one?

context.heading: Don't trip over the Messiah
context.body: Skandalizō comes from skandalon, the trigger stick of a trap. Jesus gently warns John not to be tripped up because the Messiah is healing the blind rather than toppling Herod. John's preaching had stressed coming judgment (3:10–12); Jesus points him to the mercy Isaiah also promised (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1).

context.heading: A kingdom under pressure
context.body: Verse 12 is one of the hardest in the Gospels. Biazō can mean "to use force" or "to suffer violence", so the kingdom may be forcefully advancing, violently opposed, or both. With John sitting in Herod's prison, many scholars think Jesus is acknowledging that the kingdom's arrival provokes violent resistance.

context.heading: Three towns by the lake
context.body: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum sat within a few miles of each other on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus did most of His miracles. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy pagan ports condemned by the prophets (Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus says those cities would have repented faster than His own neighbors.

theology.title: Revealed to little children
theology.body: Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to nēpioi, "infants" (v. 25). God does not hand out spiritual insight by IQ or education. Revelation is His gift, and it lands where pride is absent (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

theology.title: Only the Son knows the Father
theology.body: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son" (v. 27). It is a claim of unique, mutual knowledge, the kind of statement that shaped the church's confession of the Trinity. To know God, we come through the Son He has chosen to reveal Himself in.

application.title: When Jesus doesn't fit the plan
application.body: John expected an axe and a winnowing fork and got healings instead, while he sat in a cell. Disappointment with how God is working is not the same as unbelief, and John took his question straight to Jesus. Honest questions are better than quiet drift.
application.question: Where has Jesus not acted the way you expected, and have you actually brought that to Him?

application.title: No messenger is ever right
application.body: People called John demon-possessed for fasting and Jesus a glutton for feasting (verses 18–19). When we do not want a message, any messenger will seem wrong. Criticizing a preacher's style can be a way to avoid the content.
application.question: Whose message have you dismissed by finding fault with how they delivered it?

context.heading: The Servant who will not shout
context.body: Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1–4, the longest Old Testament quotation in his Gospel. Pais can mean child or servant, and it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the LORD's Servant in Isaiah. Matthew places it right after Jesus withdraws and tells the healed not to publicize Him: this Servant does not cry out in the streets.

context.heading: A cracked reed, a smoking wick
context.body: A kalamos was a cheap, flimsy reed; a linon was a flax wick in a clay oil lamp, smoking as it ran low. Most people would snap the reed and pinch out the wick. The Servant does neither. He is gentle with those barely holding on.

context.heading: Words that don't work
context.body: Argos means idle or useless, literally "not working". Jesus warns that even careless words will be accounted for, because the mouth speaks what fills the heart (v. 34). The Pharisees' offhand claim that Jesus drove out demons by Beelzebul was exactly this kind of word.

theology.title: Something greater is here
theology.body: Jesus says something greater than the temple (v. 6), than Jonah (v. 41) and than Solomon (v. 42) is here. Priest, prophet and king were Israel's great offices. Jesus claims to be what all three were pointing toward.

theology.title: The sign of Jonah
theology.body: Jonah's three days in the fish point to Jesus' three days in the heart of the earth (v. 40). In Jewish reckoning part of a day could count as a day, so Friday to Sunday fits. God's decisive sign would not be another miracle on demand but the resurrection.

application.title: Rules that crowd out mercy
application.body: The Pharisees were more troubled by a Sabbath healing than by a man's withered hand. Any of us can care more about how things are done than about the person in front of us. Jesus asks plainly whether it is lawful to do good (verses 10–12).
application.question: Which of your rules at home, church or work has started to matter more than the people it was meant to serve?

application.title: A swept, empty house
application.body: Jesus describes an unclean spirit returning to a house swept clean but empty, bringing seven worse (verses 43–45). Moral cleanup without a new occupant does not last. Breaking a bad habit leaves a space that something will fill.
application.question: What have you removed from your life recently, and what have you put in its place?

context.heading: Secrets now disclosed
context.body: In the Bible a mystērion is not a puzzle to crack but a secret God kept and now reveals (Daniel 2:28). The mystery of the kingdom is that God's reign has arrived in Jesus quietly, before the final judgment. Parables open this to receptive hearts and leave hardened ones puzzled, as Isaiah 6:9–10 described (vv. 14–15).

context.heading: Weeds that pass for wheat
context.body: Zizanion is usually identified as darnel, a weed that looks almost identical to wheat until it heads out. Its roots tangle with the wheat's, so pulling it early would damage the crop. Roman law even addressed sowing weeds in another man's field, so the story was believable.

context.heading: A scribe trained for the kingdom
context.body: Jesus closes with a scribe who has been mathēteuō, "discipled", for the kingdom. Like a householder bringing out treasures old and new, he holds together the Old Testament and its fulfillment in Jesus. Many think Matthew, a careful handler of Scripture, saw himself in this verse.

theology.title: A patient Judge
theology.body: The owner lets the weeds grow until harvest (v. 30). God's patience with evil is not indifference: judgment is certain, and He will do the sorting, not impatient servants. Peter says the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish (2 Peter 3:9).

theology.title: A kingdom worth everything
theology.body: The treasure and the pearl (vv. 44–46) show the kingdom's surpassing worth. Both men sell all they have, but the first does it "in his joy". Giving everything is not grim loss when you have found what is truly worth having.

application.title: Thorny ground looks busy
application.body: The seed among thorns sprouts, but the worries of life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke it (verse 22). This hearer is not hostile, just crowded. A full calendar can quietly do what persecution could not.
application.question: What concerns are drinking up the attention meant for God's word in your life right now?

application.title: Not every sorting job is yours
application.body: The servants wanted to rip out the weeds at once. The owner said wait, because they could not reliably tell the difference without damaging good plants. Some judgments belong only to God.
application.question: Where are you trying to do a sorting job that belongs to God?

context.heading: A ruler trapped by his pride
context.body: Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, not a true king, though he was popularly called one. The historian Josephus says John was held at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, because Antipas feared his influence. Antipas grieved at the request but feared losing face before his guests more than shedding innocent blood.

context.heading: A blessing over bread
context.body: Eulogeō means to speak well of, to bless. Jewish custom was to bless God before eating, with words like "Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth" (a form attested in later Jewish sources). Jesus does what every Jewish father did at the table, and five loaves become enough for thousands.

context.heading: The fourth watch
context.body: Romans divided the night into four phylakai, "watches". The fourth ran roughly from 3 to 6 a.m. The disciples had been fighting the wind for most of the night when Jesus came to them.

theology.title: A shepherd who spreads a table
theology.body: Feeding a crowd in a desolate place recalls manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16) and Elisha's multiplied loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Psalm 23 pictures the LORD as a shepherd spreading a table. Jesus does what God did for Israel, with twelve baskets left over.

theology.title: Lord over the chaos waters
theology.body: In Scripture the sea often stands for chaos and threat, and God makes a path through it (Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:16). Jesus walks on it, climbs into the boat, and the wind stops. The disciples reach the right conclusion: "Truly You are the Son of God" (v. 33), and they worship.

application.title: Withdraw, then serve
application.body: Hearing of John's death, Jesus withdrew to a solitary place, then saw the crowds and had compassion. Grief did not stop Him caring, but He did not skip the solitude either. Healthy service usually needs both.
application.question: When did you last let yourself step away to grieve or pray before pushing on?

application.title: Sinking is not the end
application.body: Peter really walked on water, then saw the wind and began to sink (verse 30). Jesus caught him "immediately". Failing halfway through a step of faith is not disqualification; it is often where we learn who is holding us.
application.question: What step of faith have you avoided because you're afraid of sinking halfway?

context.heading: A loophole called a gift
context.body: Some taught that property declared a dōron, a gift devoted to God (Mark 7:11 gives the Hebrew term, corban), could no longer be used to support one's parents. The owner might still enjoy it himself. Jesus says this tradition cancels the commandment to honor father and mother.

context.heading: What makes a person common
context.body: Koinoō, "to defile", comes from koinos, "common". To be defiled was to be made ordinary, unfit for holy use. Jesus moves defilement from the stomach to the heart (vv. 18–19): people are made unholy by what they produce, not by what they digest.

context.heading: House dogs, not strays
context.body: Jesus uses kynarion, a diminutive for household dogs or puppies, not street scavengers. The woman seizes the image: even house dogs eat the crumbs from the master's table. Jesus' words sound harsh, but they draw out a faith He then praises in public.

theology.title: Mercy past the border
theology.body: Matthew calls her a Canaanite, the name of Israel's ancient enemies. Yet she addresses Jesus as "Lord, Son of David" and receives mercy. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 22:18), and this is a foretaste.

theology.title: The God of Israel praised
theology.body: After many healings the crowd "glorified the God of Israel" (v. 31), a phrase that suits outsiders. Many scholars think this second feeding happened among largely Gentile crowds. Either way, the God who fed Israel in the wilderness keeps feeding hungry people with more than enough.

application.title: Fences that replace the field
application.body: The elders' rules began as fences to protect God's law and slowly replaced it. Families and churches still do this: a preference becomes a rule, then a test of faithfulness. Jesus asks whether our traditions serve God's commands or sidestep them.
application.question: Which tradition you hold might be getting in the way of loving someone God told you to love?

application.title: Arguing from His abundance
application.body: The woman kept asking through silence, a refusal and an apparent insult. She never claimed she deserved help; she appealed to how much Jesus had to give. That is a model for prayer when God seems quiet.
application.question: What request have you stopped bringing to God because the first answer was silence?

context.heading: The steward's keys
context.body: Kleis, "key", recalls Isaiah 22:22, where the palace steward Eliakim receives the key of David's house to open and shut. A steward controlled access on the king's behalf. Christians differ on whether and how Peter's role continues, but many see it exercised as he opened the door of the gospel to Jews (Acts 2) and Gentiles (Acts 10).

context.heading: Binding and loosing
context.body: "Bind" (deō) and "loose" were rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, or for declaring someone guilty or free. The Greek can be read "will have been bound" in heaven, suggesting the church recognizes on earth what heaven has already decided. The same authority is given to the gathered community in 18:18.

context.heading: From rock to stumbling stone
context.body: Minutes after being called a rock, Peter becomes a skandalon, a stone to trip over, by rebuking Jesus for speaking of the cross. Jesus calls him "Satan" because he is repeating the wilderness offer of a crown without suffering (4:8–10). Peter has the right title for Jesus and the wrong idea of what it means.

theology.title: The living God reveals His Son
theology.body: Peter's confession did not come from "flesh and blood" but from the Father (v. 17). In a city full of shrines to idols and to Caesar, Peter names the Son of the living God. Knowing who Jesus is remains a gift of revelation, not just the result of a debate.

theology.title: The cross was always the plan
theology.body: From this point Jesus began to show that He must suffer, die and be raised (v. 21). "Must" (dei) speaks of divine necessity, rooted in passages like Isaiah 53. Messiahship and suffering, which Peter thought were opposites, belong together in God's plan.

application.title: Disown the self in charge
application.body: Aparneomai, "deny" (verse 24), is the same verb used for Peter's denials of Jesus (26:34). Jesus is not talking about giving up dessert; He means disowning self as the one in charge. That reaches into how we spend Saturdays, budget, argue and scroll.
application.question: In what area do you still act as though your preferences are the final authority?

application.title: Smaller prizes than the world
application.body: Jesus asks what it profits to gain the whole world and forfeit your soul (verse 26). Few of us are close to gaining the world. We tend to trade our souls for much smaller prizes: a promotion, an image, an argument won.
application.question: What prize far smaller than the world are you most tempted to trade your soul for?

context.heading: Three booths on a mountain
context.body: Peter offers to build three skēnai, "tents" or "booths". The word recalls the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in booths to remember the wilderness, and the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. Peter may have wanted the moment to last, but he also put Moses and Elijah on a level with Jesus.

context.heading: The bright cloud speaks
context.body: The nephelē, "cloud", that overshadows them recalls the glory cloud that led Israel and filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). From it comes the Father's voice. "Listen to Him!" echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promised a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear.

context.heading: Do sons pay the tax?
context.body: Jewish men paid a yearly half-shekel for the temple (Exodus 30:13), equal to a didrachmon, "two drachmas". Jesus says kings' sons are exempt, implying He is the Son of the temple's King. Yet to avoid offense He pays, with a coin from a fish's mouth that covers Peter too.

theology.title: Glory veiled, then glimpsed
theology.body: On the mountain the disciples see what was always true: the glory of God's Son, usually veiled in ordinary flesh. Peter later wrote that he was an eyewitness of His majesty (2 Peter 1:16–18). The cross ahead does not cancel this glory; it is the road on which it is revealed.

theology.title: Elijah has already come
theology.body: The scribes expected Elijah to come before the Messiah (Malachi 4:5–6). Jesus says Elijah came in John the Baptist and was rejected, just as the Son of Man will be (vv. 12–13). God keeps His promises, often in ways the experts fail to recognize.

application.title: Life below the mountain
application.body: Peter wanted to camp on the summit, but the next scene is a desperate father and a failed ministry at the bottom. Spiritual highs are real gifts, but discipleship is mostly lived in the valley. The voice said "Listen to Him", not "Stay here".
application.question: Are you waiting for the next spiritual high instead of obeying in the ordinary valley you are in?

application.title: Rights you can lay down
application.body: Jesus had every right not to pay the tax, yet paid it "so that we may not offend them" (verse 27). Having a right does not require using it. Love sometimes sets aside a legitimate freedom for someone else's sake.
application.question: Which of your rights are you insisting on at someone else's expense?

context.heading: A donkey-sized millstone
context.body: Jesus mentions a mylos onikos, literally a "donkey millstone", the heavy upper stone turned by an animal rather than a small hand mill. Drowning with one tied on meant no rescue and no body to bury. Jesus reaches for the most extreme image available to describe harming the vulnerable.

context.heading: The sheep that wanders
context.body: Planaō means to wander or be led astray. In Luke 15 the lost sheep is a sinner outside the fold; here it is one of the "little ones" inside the community who drifts. The shepherd still leaves the ninety-nine to go after it.

context.heading: Bring it into the light
context.body: Elenchō means to expose or bring to light, usually to convince. Jesus prescribes a private conversation first, then one or two others, then the church (vv. 15–17), echoing the witnesses of Deuteronomy 19:15. The goal is "you have won your brother", not winning the argument.

theology.title: Not one of these lost
theology.body: "Your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish" (v. 14). God's attention goes to the overlooked and the wandering. Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who ignored strays and promises that God Himself will search for them.

theology.title: Present where two or three gather
theology.body: Jesus promises to be among two or three gathered in His name (v. 20). A Jewish saying (Mishnah Avot 3:2) held that God's presence rests on two who study the law together; Jesus speaks of His own presence. It anticipates His final promise to be with His people always (28:20).

application.title: Talk to them, not about them
application.body: Jesus' first step is a private conversation, not a text to a mutual friend or a vague post online. Most conflicts in families and churches escalate because we skip that step. It takes more courage to speak to someone than about them.
application.question: Who have you talked about this month that you have never actually talked to?

application.title: Remember the size of your debt
application.body: The servant forgiven an unpayable fortune throttled a man over a hundred denarii, roughly a hundred days' wages. That was a real debt, just tiny by comparison. Unforgiveness grows when we forget what we have been forgiven.
application.question: Whose debt against you are you still collecting, and how does it compare with what God has released you from?

context.heading: For any reason at all?
context.body: The Pharisees ask whether divorce is allowed for any aitia, "cause". Rabbis debated Deuteronomy 24:1: the school of Shammai allowed divorce mainly for sexual unfaithfulness, while the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any displeasure, reportedly even a spoiled meal. It was a live controversy, and they hoped to pin Jesus to a side.

context.heading: A concession, not the design
context.body: Moses permitted divorce because of sklērokardia, "hardness of heart". The law regulated a broken practice, requiring a written certificate that gave a divorced woman some protection and freedom to remarry. Jesus says that concession was never the original design.

context.heading: The renewal of all things
context.body: Palingenesia means "rebirth" or "regeneration". Here it describes the renewed creation, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne. The Twelve judging Israel's twelve tribes signals that God is restoring His people, not abandoning His promises.

theology.title: Marriage is God's work
theology.body: Jesus answers a legal question by returning to Genesis 1:27 and 2:24. God made them male and female and Himself joins husband and wife as one flesh. Christians differ on what exceptions Jesus allows (v. 9) and how they apply today, but all agree He raised the standard rather than lowering it.

theology.title: Possible only with God
theology.body: When the disciples ask who can be saved, Jesus says, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (v. 26). The rich young man was trying to do enough good; Jesus points away from effort to grace. The God who did the impossible for Sarah (Genesis 18:14) does it in every salvation.

application.title: The one thing you won't sell
application.body: The young man had kept the commandments and still lacked one thing. Jesus put His finger on the possession that possessed him. He does not ask everyone to sell everything, but He does ask about the thing we would never let go.
application.question: If Jesus named the one thing you would walk away sad over, what would it be?

application.title: Children are not interruptions
application.body: The disciples rebuked people for bringing children, as though Jesus had more important work. Children had little status, and adults came first. Jesus says the kingdom belongs to such as these.
application.question: Who at home or at church do you treat as an interruption to the work you think really matters?

context.heading: An envious eye
context.body: The owner literally asks, "Is your eye evil (ponēros) because I am good?" In Jewish idiom an evil eye meant envy or stinginess (compare 6:22–23). The all-day workers were not cheated; they were offended that the owner was generous to someone else.

context.heading: The cup He would drink
context.body: In the prophets the potērion, "cup", often stands for God's wrath poured out on sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). James and John glibly answer, "We can." Jesus would soon pray in Gethsemane for this cup to pass (26:39). They would share His suffering, but only He would drink the judgment.

context.heading: Power that presses down
context.body: Katakyrieuō means to lord it over, with a prefix that adds the sense of pressing down on others. Rulers from Rome to the local Herods used power to protect their own status. Jesus says it will not be so among His followers: the great one is the diakonos, the servant (v. 26).

theology.title: Grace is not payroll
theology.body: The landowner pays a full day's wage to those who worked one hour. God's kingdom does not run on merit pay but on His generosity. It echoes how God chose Israel not because they were many or deserving but because He loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8).

theology.title: The Servant who pays the ransom
theology.body: "The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (v. 28). The saying joins Daniel 7's exalted Son of Man with Isaiah 53's Servant who bears the sin of many. The King of glory pays the price of freedom Himself.

application.title: When others get the same grace
application.body: The early workers grumbled not because they were underpaid but because others were overpaid. We can resent a late convert, a sibling's easier road or a coworker's undeserved break. Envy keeps careful score of someone else's blessings.
application.question: Whose blessing have you resented because you felt you had earned more?

application.title: Lobbying for the best seats
application.body: James and John, with their mother's help, lobbied for the top seats, and the other ten were indignant, probably because they wanted the same ones. Jesus redefined greatness as serving. Nobody fights over that position.
application.question: Where are you competing for position when you could be looking for a way to serve?

context.heading: A hideout for robbers
context.body: Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. A lēstēs was a bandit, and the word was later used of violent rebels; a bandits' den was where robbers retreated to feel safe after their crimes. Jeremiah's point was that people sinned all week, then hid in the temple as if it protected them, shortly before Babylon destroyed it.

context.heading: All leaves, no figs
context.body: Many scholars note that a fig tree (sykē) in full leaf in spring often carried small early figs, so its leaves advertised food. This tree promised what it did not deliver. Set between temple scenes, the cursing is widely read as an acted parable of judgment on fruitless religion (compare Jeremiah 8:13).

context.heading: The stone the builders rejected
context.body: Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23, the same psalm the crowds sang at His entry (v. 9). The "head of the corner" (gōnia, "corner") was the key stone binding two walls, or possibly a capstone. Israel's leaders, the builders, are rejecting the very stone God has chosen to hold His house together.

theology.title: The gentle King arrives
theology.body: Zechariah 9:9–10 promised a king "gentle and riding on a donkey" who would end war and speak peace to the nations. Jesus deliberately acts it out. God's King comes not on a war horse to crush Rome but humbly, to make peace through His own sacrifice.

theology.title: The patient vineyard owner
theology.body: The parable of the tenants (vv. 33–41) builds on Isaiah 5:1–7, where Israel is God's vineyard. The owner sends servant after servant, then his own son. It traces God's long patience through the prophets and the climax of His love in sending His Son.

application.title: What fills your temple courts
application.body: The sellers may have offered a needed service, but they filled the space where Gentiles could pray. Good activity can crowd out the very thing a place is for. A life can be busy with useful things and have no room left for prayer.
application.question: What useful thing has taken over the space in your life meant for meeting with God?

application.title: The son who actually went
application.body: In the parable of two sons (verses 28–31), one refuses and then obeys, while the other agrees and never goes. Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom ahead of religious leaders. What counts is which son went to the vineyard.
application.question: What have you told God yes about but never actually done?

context.heading: Dressed for the wedding
context.body: A guest arrives without wedding clothes (endyma gamou, "garment of the wedding"). Some scholars suggest a king might supply festive garments, though the evidence is uncertain. Either way, the man accepted the feast while treating the host's honor casually, and the invitation did not cover that.

context.heading: Caesar's head tax
context.body: Kēnsos comes from the Latin census: a poll tax Rome required from subject peoples, paid in Roman coin. Its introduction in Judea in AD 6 sparked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean. The denarius of Tiberius carried an inscription calling his father Augustus divine, which many Jews found offensive.

context.heading: David calls Him Lord
context.body: Jesus quotes Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New. If David, speaking by the Spirit, calls the Messiah "my Lord" (kyrios), how can the Messiah be merely his son? The answer Jesus leaves hanging: the Messiah is David's descendant and far greater than David.

theology.title: The God of the living
theology.body: Against the Sadducees, Jesus cites Exodus 3:6: centuries after Abraham died, God still said "I am the God of Abraham" (v. 32). God's covenant bond with His people does not end at the grave. Resurrection hope rests on God's faithfulness to those He has bound to Himself.

theology.title: An invitation thrown open
theology.body: When the invited guests refuse, the king sends servants into the streets to gather everyone they can find, both evil and good (v. 10). God's invitation to His Son's wedding feast goes out widely, echoing Isaiah 25:6. Yet it must be received on the King's terms.

application.title: Too busy for the feast
application.body: The first guests did not hate the king; they went off, one to his field and another to his business (verse 5). Most people who turn God down are not rebelling, just distracted. Ordinary priorities can quietly decline an extraordinary invitation.
application.question: What ordinary priority has been answering God's invitation on your behalf lately?

application.title: Love God with your mind
application.body: Jesus' summary of the greatest commandment includes loving God with all your mind (verse 37). Loving God involves thinking: reading carefully, asking hard questions, refusing lazy answers. Faith is not the opposite of thought.
application.question: When did you last bring your full mind to a question about God instead of settling for a slogan?

context.heading: Bigger boxes, longer tassels
context.body: Phylaktēria were small leather boxes holding Scripture passages, bound on the arm and forehead in response to Deuteronomy 6:8. The practice itself was faithful. Jesus' complaint is that some enlarged them so their devotion could be seen from across the street.

context.heading: Tithing the spice rack
context.body: The law required tithes on grain, wine and oil (Deuteronomy 14:22–23), and some extended it to garden herbs like mint, dill and cumin. Jesus does not mock that care; He says they should have done it. He condemns neglecting the weightier matters: justice, mercy and faithfulness.

context.heading: Whitewashed tombs
context.body: Tombs were whitewashed (koniaō) so travelers could see and avoid them, since touching a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16). Later Jewish sources say this was done each spring before Passover, when pilgrims crowded into Jerusalem. Jesus' picture: gleaming outside, full of death inside.

theology.title: One Teacher, one Father
theology.body: Jesus tells His followers not to seek titles like rabbi, father or instructor, because there is one Teacher, the Christ, and one Father in heaven (vv. 8–10). Christians differ on whether this forbids certain titles or the pride behind them. Either way, ultimate authority belongs to God alone.

theology.title: Judgment from rejected love
theology.body: After seven woes, Jesus says, "How often I have longed to gather your children together" (v. 37). He speaks as the God who sent the prophets, much as the LORD grieves over rebellious Israel in Hosea 11:8. Judgment here comes not from cold anger but from love refused.

application.title: Strain the gnat, gulp the camel
application.body: Jesus' picture is comic: carefully filtering a gnat out of your drink, then swallowing a camel (verse 24). Both were unclean animals. We can obsess over small rule-keeping while missing huge failures of mercy or honesty.
application.question: What small thing are you meticulous about while ignoring something much bigger?

application.title: Craving the front row
application.body: The scribes loved the best seats and respectful greetings in the marketplace. That hunger shows up today in follower counts, titles and who gets thanked from the stage. Jesus says the greatest among you will be your servant (verse 11).
application.question: Where do you most want to be noticed, and what does that reveal about you?

context.heading: Labor pains, not the end
context.body: Ōdin means the pain of childbirth. Wars, famines and earthquakes are "the beginning of birth pains", not the end itself. Jewish writers used the image for troubles before the age of the Messiah; the pains are real, but they signal something being born (Romans 8:22).

context.heading: The abomination of desolation
context.body: Bdelygma, "abomination", names something detestable to God, especially idolatry. The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), and many Jews saw it fulfilled when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC. Many link Jesus' warning to Rome's armies in AD 70; others also expect a further, future fulfillment.

context.heading: Which generation?
context.body: Genea normally means the people living at one time. Read that way, "this generation will not pass away" fits the temple's fall about forty years later. Others read it as "this kind of people" or as the generation that sees the final signs. It is one of the most debated verses in the Gospels.

theology.title: The Lord of history
theology.body: Jesus speaks calmly about wars, false messiahs and the temple's fall before any of it happens. History is not spinning out of control; it is moving toward the Son of Man coming on the clouds (v. 30; Daniel 7:13–14). His words will outlast heaven and earth (v. 35).

theology.title: An unknown day, a certain coming
theology.body: No one knows the day or hour, "nor the Son" in His earthly mission, "but only the Father" (v. 36). Christians hold different views on the timeline of the end, but agree on its certainty and its purpose. God has set the day; our part is faithfulness, not prediction.

application.title: Love that slowly cools
application.body: Jesus warns that as wickedness multiplies, the love of most will grow cold (verse 12). The verb pictures something losing heat little by little. Cynicism about a broken world can quietly chill our love for the people in it.
application.question: What news or frustration has been cooling your love for people lately?

application.title: Faithful when the master is late
application.body: The wicked servant tells himself, "My master will be away a long time," and starts mistreating others (verses 48–49). Delay reveals what we actually believe. The faithful servant is simply found doing the job he was given.
application.question: If Jesus returned today, what would He find you doing with the responsibilities He has given you?

context.heading: Torches for a night procession
context.body: Lampas often means a torch, and many scholars think these were sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags that burned only a short while. Wedding processions often moved through the streets at night as the groom came for his bride. Without a flask of extra oil, a torch would sputter out just as he arrived.

context.heading: Not careful, just idle
context.body: The master calls the third servant ponēros and oknēros, "wicked" and "lazy" (or "hesitant"). Burying money was a common way to guard valuables, so he had kept it safe. His fault was not losing the talent but doing nothing with it, because he saw his master as harsh.

context.heading: A mixed flock at evening
context.body: In Palestine sheep and goats (eriphos) often grazed together in one flock by day, and from a distance could look much alike. Shepherds commonly separated them at evening. The picture is of people who mingle all their lives until the Shepherd-King sorts them.

theology.title: The King beside the least
theology.body: The Son of Man sits on His glorious throne with all nations before Him (vv. 31–32), echoing Daniel 7:13–14. Yet He measures people by how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner. Christians differ on whether "the least of these" means needy people generally or needy believers, but either way the King takes it personally.

theology.title: Judgment that is real
theology.body: The chapter ends with eternal punishment and eternal life side by side (v. 46). Jesus speaks of judgment more than anyone else in Scripture, as a warning given in love. Salvation is by grace, yet the deeds He lists are the fruit by which living faith is seen (James 2:17).

application.title: Oil can't be borrowed
application.body: The foolish bridesmaids tried to borrow oil at the last minute and were refused. Some things cannot be transferred, like a parent's faith or a spouse's prayer life. Readiness for Jesus is personal.
application.question: Are you leaning on a parent's, spouse's or pastor's faith instead of your own?

application.title: Fear buries gifts
application.body: The third servant said, "I was afraid and went out and hid your talent" (verse 25). Fear of failure, or of a harsh God, can freeze us into doing nothing. Jesus treats that inaction as a real failure, not a safe choice.
application.question: What ability or opportunity have you buried because you were afraid of doing it badly?

application.title: Mercy that keeps no record
application.body: Both groups are surprised: "Lord, when did we see You?" The righteous were not performing for Jesus; they simply helped the person in front of them. Real mercy rarely keeps a scorecard of itself.
application.question: Who is the overlooked person in your week who might be the place you meet Christ?

context.heading: The price of a slave
context.body: Thirty argyria, "pieces of silver", was the compensation owed for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32). In Zechariah 11:12–13 a shepherd of God's people is paid off with thirty pieces, an insulting wage that is thrown to the potter. Matthew sees the Lord's own Shepherd valued at the price of a slave.

context.heading: Grief that surrounds Him
context.body: Perilypos means hemmed in by grief, overwhelmed with sorrow. Jesus' words echo Psalms 42–43: "Why, my soul, are you downcast?" He is not serene and detached before His death. He feels its full weight and asks His friends to stay awake with Him.

context.heading: A kiss that betrays
context.body: Judas arranged to identify Jesus with a kiss (phileō, v. 48), a normal greeting from disciple to teacher. When he arrives, Matthew uses kataphileō, which can suggest a warm or lingering kiss. The intimacy deepens the betrayal, echoing Psalm 41:9: even a close friend has lifted his heel against me.

theology.title: The true Passover Lamb
theology.body: Jesus reinterprets the Passover meal around Himself: the bread His body, the cup His blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins (vv. 26–28). As the lamb's blood once marked Israel's doors for rescue, His death now rescues a new people. Christians differ on how Christ is present in the Lord's Supper, but all see it proclaiming His death.

theology.title: Yes in a garden
theology.body: "Yet not as I will, but as You will" (v. 39). In Gethsemane the Son's human will genuinely recoils from the cup and freely submits to the Father. Adam said no in a garden; Jesus says yes in one. His obedience to death is the heart of our salvation (Philippians 2:8).

application.title: Waste or worship?
application.body: The disciples called the woman's perfume a waste that could have helped the poor. Jesus called it a beautiful deed (verse 10). Some love for Jesus will look impractical to sensible people.
application.question: What would it look like for you to love Jesus in a way others might call excessive?

application.title: Intentions need habits
application.body: The disciples meant well and fell asleep anyway. Jesus' answer was not shame but a practical instruction: watch and pray so that you will not enter temptation (verse 41). Willing spirits still need practices that hold them up.
application.question: Where do your good intentions keep collapsing because nothing practical is holding them up?

context.heading: Remorse without return
context.body: Judas was filled with metamelomai, remorse or regret. Matthew does not use metanoeō, the repentance John and Jesus preached (3:2; 4:17). Judas felt terrible and returned the money, but there is no sign he turned to God for mercy. Peter also failed badly, wept, and was later restored.

context.heading: Washing his hands
context.body: Aponiptō means to wash off. Deuteronomy 21:6–7 describes elders washing their hands to declare innocence over an unsolved killing. Pilate, a Gentile, makes a similar public gesture, yet he alone had the authority to stop the execution. Water does not remove responsibility.

context.heading: "Why have You forsaken Me?"
context.body: Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22. Egkataleipō means to abandon someone in a desperate situation. Psalm 22 moves from abandonment to rescue and worship among the nations (22:27), and many scholars think Jesus had the whole psalm in view, even as He truly felt the weight of sin's separation.

theology.title: Forsaken so we could be welcomed
theology.body: The sinless Son cries out as one abandoned, bearing the judgment our sin deserved (Isaiah 53:6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Christians affirm that the Trinity was not torn apart, yet Jesus truly experienced sin's curse in His humanity. His abandonment is the ground of our welcome.

theology.title: Whose blood, and for whom
theology.body: The crowd shouts, "His blood be on us and on our children!" (v. 25). Some Christians later twisted this verse to justify hatred of Jews, a grievous misuse. Matthew, himself Jewish, records a crowd in one moment, not a curse on a people; the New Testament places all humanity under guilt for the cross and offers His blood for forgiveness (26:28).

theology.title: The turning point of history
theology.body: The earth shakes, tombs open and some saints are raised (vv. 51–53), unusual verses that recall Ezekiel 37. Jesus' death is not merely a tragedy but the hinge of God's plan. A Gentile soldier becomes the first to confess Him as God's Son after He dies (v. 54).

application.title: The convenient sin
application.body: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent, got a warning from his wife, and still handed Him over because a riot was brewing. His sin was not hatred but convenience. Many wrongs are done by people protecting a job or a reputation.
application.question: Where are you tempted to do what is easy rather than what you know is right because people are watching?

application.title: The ones who stayed
application.body: Many women watched from a distance, and Joseph of Arimathea risked his standing to ask for the body (verses 55–58). When the disciples scattered, these followers stayed and served at the worst moment. Sometimes faithfulness is simply refusing to leave.
application.question: Who in your life is in a dark season that you need to stay present for?

context.heading: Feet you can grasp
context.body: The women krateō, "take hold of", Jesus' feet and worship Him. Matthew stresses that the risen Jesus has a real body you can touch, not a ghost or a vision. In a culture where women's testimony counted for less in court, it is striking that they are the first witnesses, a detail unlikely to be invented.

context.heading: One name, three persons
context.body: Jesus commands baptizing in the onoma, "name", singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. One name shared by three is among the clearest Trinitarian statements in the Gospels. Baptism into someone's name meant coming under their ownership and protection.

context.heading: Until the age is complete
context.body: Synteleia means completion or consummation. The same phrase, "the end of the age", appears in the disciples' question about His return (24:3). Jesus' presence covers every century between Easter and that day, including this one.

theology.title: Resurrection is God's verdict
theology.body: The resurrection is the Father's public reversal of the cross. Psalm 16:10 promised that God's Holy One would not see decay, and Peter preached it fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 2:31). Jesus' claims to be the Son and the coming Judge were not idle boasts; God vindicated them.

theology.title: All authority, all nations
theology.body: Daniel 7:14 promised the Son of Man dominion over all peoples, nations and languages. Jesus now claims all authority in heaven and on earth and sends His followers to all nations. God's promise to bless every family of the earth through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) is being kept through this mission.

application.title: Sent with doubts still in hand
application.body: On the mountain they worshiped, "but some doubted" (verse 17). Jesus did not wait for flawless faith before giving the commission. He sent worshipers who still had questions.
application.question: What doubt have you assumed disqualifies you from being sent?

application.title: Fear and joy together
application.body: The women ran from the tomb "in fear and great joy" (verse 8). Meeting the risen Jesus did not erase their fear at once; it set joy beside it. You do not have to feel fearless to obey.
application.question: What would you do this week if you obeyed Jesus while still afraid?
